cards.meaning: Assign a value to a variable (no spaces around =)
cards.example: var2="one two three"; var3=one\ two\ three
cards.notes: Quote or backslash-escape if the value has spaces. Partial quoting keeps spaces as one word.

cards.meaning: Expand to the variable’s value
cards.notes: Both mean the value. Braces required when the name would run into other characters (${var}s) or for ${10}.

cards.meaning: Indirect referencing — the variable named by $var
cards.notes: var holds the name value; value holds hello; $b becomes hello. Extra $ so Bash takes the variable named by $var.

cards.meaning: Exact synonyms — modify properties of variables
cards.notes: Bash does not segregate variables by type by default; declare/typeset change properties.

cards.meaning: Treat the variable as an integer
cards.notes: Same as typeset -i. Without it, n=6/3 stays the string 6/3; with it, n is 2. Default Bash variables are character strings.

cards.meaning: Length of the string in characters
cards.notes: # inside ${} = how many characters.

cards.meaning: Length of the first array element — not the element count
cards.notes: Result is 1 (length of a), not 3. Element count is ${#array[@]}.

cards.meaning: Substring — extract length characters at position (0-based)
cards.notes: Position 2 is c; five characters → cABC1.

cards.meaning: Strip shortest match of Pattern from the front
cards.notes: → 123ABCabc. # eats the head; one # = shortest.

cards.meaning: Strip longest match of Pattern from the front
cards.notes: → abc. Two ## = greedy prefix strip.

cards.meaning: Strip shortest match of Pattern from the back
cards.notes: → abcABC123ABC. % eats the tail; one % = shortest.

cards.meaning: Strip longest match of Pattern from the back
cards.notes: → a. Two %% = greedy suffix strip.

cards.meaning: Replace the first match of Pattern with Replacement
cards.notes: → xyzABC123ABCabc. Omit Replacement to delete the first match (${stringZ/abc} → ABC123ABCabc). Case-sensitive (ABC ≠ abc).

cards.meaning: Replace all matches of Pattern with Replacement
cards.notes: → xyzABC123ABCxyz. Omit Replacement to delete all matches (${stringZ//abc} → ABC123ABC).

cards.meaning: Replace only if Pattern matches the prefix
cards.notes: → XYZABC123ABCabc. /# = front only (# = head).

cards.meaning: Replace only if Pattern matches the suffix
cards.notes: → abcABC123ABCXYZ. /% = end only (% = tail).

cards.meaning: If parameter unset, use default (do not assign)
cards.notes: Unset → default. Declared-but-null does not use the default (empty stays empty).

cards.meaning: If parameter unset or null, use default (do not assign)
cards.notes: Extra : = also when declared but empty. Common for missing command-line args (generic.data).

cards.meaning: If parameter unset, set it to default
cards.notes: Writes the default into the variable when unset. Declared-but-null does not assign.

cards.meaning: If parameter unset or null, set it to default
cards.notes: → abc, and varZ is now abc. Extra : = also when empty.

cards.meaning: If parameter is set (even empty), use alt_value
cards.notes: Unset → empty. Set-but-empty → xyz. Opposite job from -.

cards.meaning: If parameter is set and not empty, use alt_value
cards.notes: Set-but-empty → empty. Set-and-nonempty → alt. Extra : = must also be non-empty.

cards.meaning: If parameter unset, print err_msg and abort with status 1
cards.notes: If set, use it. The : null command evaluates substitutions for side effect. Unset → die before later echoes.

cards.meaning: If parameter unset or null, print err_msg and abort with status 1
cards.notes: Extra : = empty counts as missing too.

cards.meaning: Without : = only unset; with : = unset or null
cards.notes: Colon cheat sheet for parameter substitution. Declared-but-null differs only when : is present.

cards.meaning: Variable visible only within a function (or code block)
cards.notes: Only valid in a function. Without local, a name set inside leaks outside.

cards.meaning: Put a variable in the environment for this session and children
cards.notes: Affects the shell and child processes.

cards.meaning: List current environment variables
cards.notes: Shows names like HOSTNAME, PATH, USER, SHELL, …

cards.meaning: Load environment (or other) settings into the current shell during a script
cards.notes: Same idea as source. Variables stay in this shell.

cards.meaning: Where environment variables are commonly set
cards.notes: /etc/environment = system-wide. ~/.bashrc and ~/.bash_profile = all sessions of a user. export = current session.

cards.meaning: Default editor invoked by a script (usually vi or emacs)
cards.notes: Common environment / built-in name from the course table.

cards.meaning: Home directory of the user (usually /home/username)
cards.notes: Common environment variable.

cards.meaning: System host name (assigned at bootup via hostname in an init script)
cards.notes: Machine name from boot / hostname.

cards.meaning: Internal field separator — what splits words
cards.notes: Affects how the shell splits fields.

cards.meaning: Path to binaries — search path for commands
cards.notes: Where the shell looks for executables.

cards.meaning: Pseudorandom integer in the range 0–32767 (not a constant)
cards.notes: Internal Bash function; a new number each time you expand it.

cards.meaning: Name of the script itself
cards.example: bash script.sh 1 apple → $0 is script.sh (or the path used)
cards.notes: Not counted among the looped arguments in a typical for arg in $@ loop.

cards.meaning: Positional parameters — arguments from the command line
cards.notes: $1 is the first argument, $2 the second, and so on.

cards.meaning: Tenth (and later) positional — braces required after $9
cards.notes: After $9, arguments must be enclosed in brackets: ${10}, ${11}, ${12}.

cards.meaning: Number of command-line arguments / positional parameters
cards.notes: Does not include $0.

cards.meaning: All positional parameters as a single word
cards.notes: Denotes all positionals. Prefer "$@" when each argument must stay its own word.

cards.meaning: All positional parameters as separate words
cards.example: for arg in "$@"; do echo "$arg"; done
cards.notes: Each argument stays its own word (spaces preserved when quoted).

cards.meaning: Return value — exit status of the last command
cards.notes: Covered further in the exit-codes topic.

cards.meaning: Process ID (PID) of the script
cards.notes: This shell’s PID.

cards.meaning: Flags passed to the script (using set)
cards.notes: Current set flags.

cards.meaning: Last argument of the previous command
cards.notes: Special built-in / shell variable.

cards.meaning: PID of the last job run in the background
cards.notes: Background job PID — not the script’s own $$.

cards.meaning: Initialize an array with multiple values
cards.example: my_array=( zero one two three four five )
cards.notes: Zero-based; first element is index 0. No maximum size; members need not be contiguous.

cards.meaning: Assign one array element by index
cards.notes: Any variable may be used as an array. Index 6 is the seventh slot.

cards.meaning: Introduce an array by an explicit statement
cards.notes: Alternative to compound assignment ( a b c ).

cards.meaning: Dereference one array element (braces required)
cards.notes: → six. Curly bracket notation is required.

cards.meaning: Refer all array elements
cards.notes: Both expand to every element. A session that also did my_array[6]=six includes six in the listing.

cards.meaning: Number of elements in the array
cards.notes: Element count. Contrast ${#arr} without [@] = length of element 0 only.
